title: Describing People and Things
overview: You can already compare two things — Unit 4 gave you bigger, cheaper, better. This unit gives you the top of the scale, the words for what people are like rather than what they look like, and the form that describes how something is done rather than what it is. It ends with two written references for the same person, because character words are the ones that carry weight in writing, and reading them accurately is a skill of its own.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 2 has a spelling rule worth writing out by hand.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is two references for the same person.
Do the Practice. Practice 3 is where adverbs usually go wrong.
Record yourself describing a person in character and in appearance.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
Four patterns in this unit, and three of them are extensions of something you already have.
First, character and appearance, which is vocabulary rather than grammar, but the distinction matters.
Appearance is what somebody looks like. Tall, short, thin, with curly hair, with glasses, with a beard.
Character is what somebody is like. Kind, honest, lazy, confident, shy, clever.
English keeps these apart more than you might expect, and mixing them sounds odd. If somebody asks what is she like, they want character. If they ask what does she look like, they want appearance. Those two questions look almost identical and they ask for completely different answers, so it is worth learning them as a pair. What is she like — character. What does she look like — appearance.
One warning. Describing people's appearance is normal in some situations and rude in others. Describing someone as thin or fat is not neutral in English. Thin can be a compliment or a criticism depending entirely on tone, and there is no safe version of the other word. In this unit you will practise appearance vocabulary for situations where it is genuinely needed — finding somebody in a crowd, describing a lost bag's owner — and character vocabulary for everything else. That is also how careful speakers actually use them.
Second pattern: superlatives. The top of the scale.
In Unit 4 you learned comparatives — bigger, cheaper, more expensive. That compares two things. A superlative compares one thing against all the others.
The rules run exactly parallel to Unit 4, which is the good news.
Short word: add -est and put the in front. Big, bigger, the biggest. Cheap, cheaper, the cheapest.
Long word: use the most. Expensive, more expensive, the most expensive. Interesting, more interesting, the most interesting.
And the same irregulars you already know. Good, better, the best. Bad, worse, the worst.
The word the is not optional. It is the biggest, never it is biggest. That is the most common error with this pattern and it is worth fixing early.
Spelling. Same three rules as Unit 4. Big doubles the g — the biggest. Words ending in e just add -st — the nicest. Words ending in consonant plus y change to i — the easiest, the busiest.
Third pattern: adverbs of manner. These say how something is done.
The rule is almost embarrassingly simple: take the adjective and add -ly.
Quick becomes quickly. Quiet becomes quietly. Polite becomes politely. Careful becomes carefully.
And the point of them is a distinction English cares about. An adjective describes a thing. An adverb describes an action.
She is a careful driver — careful describes her, a person.
She drives carefully — carefully describes the driving, an action.
Same idea, two forms, and which one you need depends on whether you are describing a noun or a verb.
There is one important irregular and you will use it constantly. The adverb of good is not goodly. It is well.
He is a good worker. He works well.
And a small spelling note: adjectives ending in y change to -ily. Easy becomes easily. Happy becomes happily. Adjectives already ending in -ly, like friendly, have no adverb form at all — you say in a friendly way instead.
Fourth pattern: as … as. This says two things are equal.
She is as tall as her brother. This job is as hard as the last one.
The structure is fixed: as, then the adjective, then as. Nothing changes the adjective — no -er, no -est, no more. That is what people get wrong: as bigger as, or as more tall as. It is just as tall as.
And the negative is extremely useful: not as … as means less than.
This job is not as hard as the last one. That means it is easier. It is a softer way of saying easier, and English uses it constantly.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: Caring about other people and wanting to help them.

readings.title: What Is She Like, and What Does She Look Like
readings.passage:
Two English questions look almost identical and ask for completely different things.
What is she like? asks about character. Answer: she is kind, she is quite shy at first, she works very hard.
What does she look like? asks about appearance. Answer: she is tall, she has short dark hair, she wears glasses.
The words are nearly the same and the difference is the verb — is, or look like. Once you have noticed it you will not confuse them again, but until you notice it, it is very easy to answer the wrong one.
And answering the wrong one is not a small error. If somebody asks what a new colleague is like, they want to know whether they will get on with them. Answering she is tall with dark hair tells them nothing they asked for, and it also sounds strange, in a way that is hard to explain if you have not heard it.
There is a third question that catches people. What does she like? — no s on look, and a completely different meaning again. That one asks about preferences: she likes tea, she likes working alone.
So: what is she like, character. What does she look like, appearance. What does she like, preferences. Three questions, five words each, and one word different between them.
They are worth learning as a set rather than one at a time, because they only become confusing when you meet them separately.

readings.title: Describing People Without Judging Them
readings.passage:
Appearance words in English are not neutral, and the ones about bodies are the least neutral of all.
There is a simple test that works most of the time. Ask why you are describing the person. If the answer is so somebody can find them, appearance words are appropriate and nobody minds: the tall man with the grey beard, the woman with the glasses. That is a description doing a job.
If there is no such job to do, appearance words start to sound like judgements, and one of them always is. Thin can be a compliment or a criticism depending entirely on the tone, and it is not safe to assume which one a listener heard. The opposite word has no safe version at all.
Careful speakers do three things. They lead with what a person is like rather than what they look like. They use appearance only where it identifies. And when they must describe a body, they choose the least loaded word available and say it plainly rather than softening it, because the softened versions usually sound worse.
There is also a practical reason to prefer character words. Appearance changes and character descriptions travel. If you tell somebody a colleague is patient and explains things twice, that is useful next month. If you tell them she has short hair, it may not be true by then.
This is not about being cautious with language for its own sake. It is that appearance descriptions are useful in a narrow set of situations and misleading everywhere else, and knowing which situation you are in is most of the skill.

readings.title: Two References for the Same Person
readings.setting: Two references written for the same job applicant by two former employers.
readings.passage:
REFERENCE A
  From: Northfield Warehouse

  I worked with Sara for two years.

  She is the most reliable member of the
  team. She arrives early, she works
  quickly, and she is calm when the shift
  is difficult.

  She is quieter than most people here and
  is sometimes shy with new staff, but she
  is not as shy as she seems - she simply
  waits to be asked.

  She is honest. When she made a mistake
  with an order she reported it herself
  before anyone noticed.

  I would employ her again.

-----------------------------------------

  REFERENCE B
  From: Central Stores

  Sara was employed here from March to
  November.

  She was punctual and her work was
  satisfactory.

  She completed the tasks she was given.

  She left of her own accord.

  I confirm the dates above are correct.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between what is she like and what does she look like?
comprehension.a: The first asks about character; the second asks about appearance. The only difference is the verb.
comprehension.why: Five words each and one word apart, which is exactly why they get confused. Noticing the verb is the whole fix.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say answering the wrong one is not a small error?
comprehension.a: Because someone asking what a colleague is like wants to know whether they will get on with them, and an appearance answer tells them nothing they asked for.
comprehension.why: The consequence is a failed exchange rather than a grammar mark. The answer is grammatically perfect and completely useless.

comprehension.q: What does what does she like ask for?
comprehension.a: Preferences — what she enjoys or wants, such as she likes tea or she likes working alone.
comprehension.why: The third question in the set, one word from the second. The text recommends learning all three together because they only confuse when met separately.

comprehension.q: What test does the text give for when appearance words are appropriate?
comprehension.a: Ask why you are describing the person. If it is so somebody can find them, appearance words are doing a job and nobody minds.
comprehension.why: It is a test of purpose rather than of vocabulary, which is why it works across situations the learner has not met yet.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say character descriptions travel better than appearance ones?
comprehension.a: Because appearance changes but character is still useful next month — she is patient and explains things twice stays true, while she has short hair may not.
comprehension.why: This is a practical argument rather than a careful one, and it is the reason that persuades people who are unmoved by the first.

comprehension.q: What three things does the text say careful speakers do?
comprehension.a: They lead with character rather than appearance, they use appearance only where it identifies, and where they must describe a body they choose the least loaded word and say it plainly.
comprehension.why: The third is the least obvious: softening a loaded word usually makes it sound worse, not better.

comprehension.q: Reference A says she is not as shy as she seems. What does not as … as mean here?
comprehension.a: Less shy than she appears — she seems shy but is less so in reality, because she simply waits to be asked.
comprehension.why: Not as … as means less than. Here it is being used to correct an impression rather than to compare two people, which is one of its most common uses.

comprehension.q: Reference B says her work was satisfactory and she completed the tasks she was given. What is it telling you?
comprehension.a: Very little that is positive. Satisfactory is the lowest acceptable word, and completed the tasks she was given says she did nothing beyond what she was told.
comprehension.why: This is the key inference in the document. Nothing in Reference B is a criticism, and the whole reference is faint praise — what is absent carries the meaning.

comprehension.q: Which reference would help Sara more, and name two specific things that make the difference?
comprehension.a: Reference A. It uses superlatives — the most reliable member of the team — and it gives evidence, such as reporting her own mistake before anyone noticed.
comprehension.why: A strong reference makes a claim at the top of a scale and then proves it with an incident. Reference B does neither, and confirms dates instead.

comprehension.q: Reference A says she is quieter than most people here. Why is that not a criticism?
comprehension.a: Because it is immediately explained — she is sometimes shy with new staff but not as shy as she seems, and she waits to be asked. The comparison sets up the correction.
comprehension.why: A comparative used honestly and then qualified reads as a fair description, which makes the praise around it more believable. Reference A is more useful precisely because it is not uniformly positive.

grammar.title: Character and appearance
grammar.explanation: Two sets of words that answer two questions which look almost identical. The words are vocabulary; the skill is telling the questions apart.
grammar.rule:
WHAT IS SHE LIKE?          -> character
  She is kind.
  She is quite shy at first.
  She works very hard.

WHAT DOES SHE LOOK LIKE?   -> appearance
  She is tall.
  She has short dark hair.
  She wears glasses.

WHAT DOES SHE LIKE?        -> preferences
  She likes working alone.

APPEARANCE STRUCTURES:
  She has  + hair / a beard
  She is   + tall / thin
  She wears / with + glasses

  the tall man with the grey beard
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody asks: what is your new colleague like?
1. Check the verb. It is is, not look like. So this is character.
2. Choose character words: kind, quiet, hard-working, clever, calm.
3. Answer: She is very calm, and she is quite quiet until you ask her something.
Now the other question: what does she look like?
1. The verb is look like, so this is appearance.
2. Use the appearance structures: She is tall, she has short dark hair, and she wears glasses.
The two answers share no words at all, which is the clearest sign they are genuinely different questions rather than two ways of asking one thing.
grammar.mistake: Answering the character question with appearance. She is tall with dark hair, in reply to what is she like, is grammatical and sounds distinctly odd, because the asker wanted to know whether they would get on with her. The other error is has and is: she is long hair. Hair takes has, height takes is.
grammar.tip: Is — character. Look like — appearance. Like — preferences.
grammar.practice:
Write CHARACTER or APPEARANCE, then answer each one in a full sentence about somebody you know.
1. What is he like?
2. What does she look like?
3. What are they like?
4. What does he look like?
5. What does she like?
6. Describe somebody so a stranger could find them in a crowd. Which set did you use, and why?
grammar.answers:
1. CHARACTER  2. APPEARANCE  3. CHARACTER  4. APPEARANCE  5. PREFERENCES
6. Appearance — because the description has a job to do, which is the test in Reading 2. Something like: the tall man with the grey beard, in the blue jacket.
Check your answers to 1 and 3 use only character words, and 2 and 4 use has, is or with. If any answer mixed the two sets, look at the verb in the question again.

grammar.title: Superlatives: the -est and the most
grammar.explanation: Unit 4 gave you comparatives, which compare two things. A superlative compares one thing against all the others. The rules run exactly parallel, so if you have Unit 4 you already have most of this.
grammar.rule:
SHORT WORD  -> the + adjective + est
  big        bigger        the biggest
  cheap      cheaper       the cheapest

LONG WORD   -> the most + adjective
  expensive  more expensive  the most expensive
  reliable   more reliable   the most reliable

IRREGULARS — the same ones as Unit 4
  good  better  the best
  bad   worse   the worst

THE IS NOT OPTIONAL
  It is the biggest.   NOT  It is biggest.

SPELLING — same three rules as Unit 4
  big   -> the biggest    (double the g)
  nice  -> the nicest     (just add -st)
  easy  -> the easiest    (y becomes i)
  busy  -> the busiest
grammar.workedExample:
Say that one member of a team is more reliable than every other.
1. One against all the others, so this is a superlative, not a comparative.
2. Is reliable short or long? Long — three syllables. So use the most.
3. Build it: the most reliable.
4. Result: She is the most reliable member of the team.
Now a short word. Say one job is harder than all the others.
1. Superlative again.
2. Hard is short, so add -est: hardest.
3. Add the, which is not optional: It is the hardest job here.
The test for short or long is the same as Unit 4: one syllable takes -est, three or more take the most, and two-syllable words split — those ending in -y take -est, most others take the most.
grammar.mistake: Leaving out the — it is biggest, she is most reliable. The is required with every superlative and it is the single most common error with this pattern. The other is doubling up: the most biggest. Choose one method, never both.
grammar.tip: The is not optional. One against all the others takes the.
grammar.practice:
Write the superlative.
1. big — It is ____ warehouse in the town.
2. reliable — She is ____ person on the team.
3. good — That was ____ interview I have had.
4. easy — This is ____ part of the job.
5. bad — It was ____ day of the week.
6. expensive — That is ____ one in the shop.
grammar.answers:
1. the biggest  2. the most reliable  3. the best  4. the easiest  5. the worst  6. the most expensive
Every answer starts with the. If any of yours did not, that is the error to fix first.
Check the spelling in 1 and 4: biggest doubles the g, and easy changes y to i before -est.

grammar.title: Adverbs of manner
grammar.explanation: These say how something is done. The form is simple — add -ly to the adjective. The skill is knowing whether the sentence needs the adjective or the adverb, and that depends on what is being described.
grammar.rule:
FORM:  adjective + ly
  quick   -> quickly
  quiet   -> quietly
  polite  -> politely
  careful -> carefully

SPELLING:  y becomes -ily
  easy    -> easily
  happy   -> happily

ONE IRREGULAR, used constantly:
  good    -> well      NOT goodly

NO ADVERB FORM AT ALL:
  friendly -> in a friendly way

WHICH ONE DOES THE SENTENCE NEED?
  adjective describes a THING (noun)
     She is a careful driver.
  adverb describes an ACTION (verb)
     She drives carefully.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that somebody does their work with care.
1. What is being described — the person, or the working? The working. That is an action.
2. Actions take adverbs, so you need the -ly form: carefully.
3. Result: She works carefully.
Now describe the person instead.
1. What is being described? Her — a noun.
2. Nouns take adjectives, so no -ly: careful.
3. Result: She is a careful worker.
The test that decides every case: find the word being described. If it is a person or thing, use the adjective. If it is a verb, use the adverb.
And remember the irregular, because it comes up constantly: he is a good worker, but he works well.
grammar.mistake: Using goodly, which does not exist — the adverb of good is well. Also using the adjective for an action: she works careful, he speaks quiet. And treating friendly as an adverb: she spoke friendly. Friendly ends in -ly but is an adjective, and there is no adverb form — say in a friendly way.
grammar.tip: Describing a thing, use the adjective. Describing an action, add -ly.
grammar.practice:
Choose the adjective or the adverb.
1. She is a (careful / carefully) driver.
2. She drives (careful / carefully).
3. He works (quick / quickly).
4. He is a (quick / quickly) worker.
5. He is a (good / well) worker.
6. He works (good / well).
7. She spoke (polite / politely).
8. She is a (polite / politely) person.
grammar.answers:
1. careful  2. carefully  3. quickly  4. quick  5. good  6. well
7. politely  8. polite
Every odd-numbered pair is the same word twice, once describing a thing and once describing an action. Find the word being described and the answer follows.
Numbers 5 and 6 are the irregular. Good describes the worker; well describes the working. There is no such word as goodly.

grammar.title: As … as
grammar.explanation: This says two things are equal. The negative says one is less, and it is used far more often than the positive.
grammar.rule:
EQUAL:
  She is as tall as her brother.
  This job is as hard as the last one.

THE ADJECTIVE NEVER CHANGES
  as tall as        NOT  as taller as
  as hard as        NOT  as more hard as

LESS — and this is the common one:
  This job is not as hard as the last one.
  = it is easier.

SOFTENING IT:
  It is almost as hard as the last one.
  It is exactly as hard as the last one.

RELATED, and each takes a different word:
  the same AS
  similar  TO
  different FROM
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say a new job is easier than your old one, but gently.
1. Easier is a comparative, which is direct. The softer way is not as … as.
2. Choose the adjective for the harder one: hard.
3. Build it: not as hard as.
4. Result: This job is not as hard as my last one.
That says exactly the same thing as this job is easier, and it lands more gently, which is why English uses it so much.
Now the positive: two jobs that are equal. She is as tall as her brother — as, adjective, as, with nothing changed about the adjective in the middle. The most common error is putting a comparative there: as taller as. The whole point of the structure is that the adjective stays plain.
grammar.mistake: Changing the adjective — as taller as, as more difficult as. Nothing goes on the adjective inside this structure. The other error is the three related words that each take a different preposition: the same as, similar to, different from. Similar as and different than are both wrong, and they are wrong in the direction of what feels natural.
grammar.tip: As, plain adjective, as. Not as … as means less.
grammar.practice:
Write the sentence.
1. Two jobs, equally hard.
2. This job, less hard than the last one.
3. Two prices, exactly equal. Use the same.
4. Two jobs, nearly but not quite equally difficult.
5. Two jobs that resemble each other. Use similar.
6. Two jobs that do not resemble each other. Use different.
grammar.answers:
1. This job is as hard as the last one.
2. This job is not as hard as the last one.
3. It costs exactly the same as the other one.
4. It is almost as difficult as the last one.
5. This job is similar to the one I did before.
6. This job is different from the one I did before.
Numbers 3, 5 and 6 use the three different prepositions: the same as, similar to, different from. Those three are worth saying aloud together until the pairing is automatic.
In 1, 2 and 4 the adjective is plain — hard, not harder.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The three questions
speaking.instructions:
Say each question five times, then answer it about somebody you know.
What is he like?
What does he look like?
What does he like?
Record all three questions and all three answers.
Play it back and check that no character word appeared in the appearance answer and no appearance word appeared in the character answer. If they mixed, listen to the verb in the question again.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor the three questions about an invented person and check the answers match the questions.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Somebody you work with
speaking.instructions:
Describe somebody you work with, or have worked with.
Six sentences of character only. No appearance at all.
Use at least four different character words and at least one superlative.
Record it.
Then listen back and ask: does this tell somebody whether they would get on with this person? If it is a list of adjectives with no example, add one incident.
speaking.tutor: Describe a colleague to the tutor and ask what kind of person it now imagines.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — The top of the scale
speaking.instructions:
Say twelve superlative sentences about things you know — the biggest, the cheapest, the best, the worst, the most difficult, the most interesting.
Six short words with -est, six long words with the most.
Record them. Play back and check every single one begins with the. That is the error this drill exists to catch.
speaking.tutor: Say twelve superlatives and ask the tutor to flag any missing the.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Thing or action
speaking.instructions:
Take six adjectives: careful, quick, quiet, polite, good, bad.
For each one, say two sentences — one describing a person and one describing what they do.
She is a careful worker. She works carefully.
Record all twelve.
Play back and check the good pair: he is a good worker, he works well. If you said goodly, say the pair ten more times.
speaking.tutor: Say pairs of sentences and ask the tutor whether each one describes a thing or an action.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Comparing two things
speaking.instructions:
Choose two things you know well — two jobs, two places you have lived, two journeys.
Say six sentences comparing them.
Use as … as once, not as … as twice, the same as once, similar to once, and different from once.
Record it.
Then listen back and check the adjective inside every as … as is plain. If you hear as harder as anywhere, that is the one thing this pattern is designed to prevent.
speaking.tutor: Compare two things to the tutor and ask it to check every as … as structure.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the references aloud and judge them
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read both references aloud, all the way through.
Then say aloud, as though explaining to a friend: which one would help Sara more, and name two specific things that make the difference.
Then say what Reference B is actually communicating, given that it criticises nothing.
Record the last two parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor both references and ask which one it would rather receive about itself.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Two descriptions of one person
writing.prompt:
Choose one person you know well.
Write two paragraphs about them.
Paragraph 1 answers what is she like — character only, at least five sentences, at least one superlative.
Paragraph 2 answers what does she look like — appearance only, at least three sentences, using has, is and with.
Then count how many words appear in both paragraphs. It should be none.
writing.model:
She is the calmest person I have worked with. When something goes wrong she does not raise her voice, and that changes the whole room. She is generous with her time — she explained the system to me three times in my first week and never suggested I should have understood it sooner. She is quite shy with people she does not know, which some people read as unfriendly, and it is not. She is honest about what she does not know, which is rarer than it sounds.
She is quite tall. She has short dark curly hair and she wears glasses. In the warehouse she always has a blue jacket on, so she is easy to find.
writing.criteria: Paragraph 1 character only, at least five sentences, at least one superlative with the; paragraph 2 appearance only, at least three sentences, using has, is and with; no word appears in both paragraphs
writing.support: Write paragraph 1 first and do not think about paragraph 2 at all until it is finished. Mixing happens when both sets of words are in your head at once.
writing.extension: Give paragraph 1 to somebody who does not know the person and ask what kind of person they imagine. Then ask what they still cannot tell.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A reference that would actually help
writing.prompt:
Write a reference for somebody — real or invented — in the shape of Reference A.
Six to ten lines.
Use at least two superlatives.
Include at least one specific incident as evidence, not just adjectives.
Include one honest qualification — something that is not entirely positive but is fairly explained.
End with a sentence saying whether you would employ them again.
writing.model:
I worked with Daniel for three years.
He is the most careful person on the team. He checks his own work before anybody asks him to, and in three years I do not remember correcting an order of his.
He works quietly and he is easy to miss in a busy room, which means he is sometimes given less credit than he should be.
He is slower than some of the others. He is also the only one who has never had to do a job twice, and I would rather have that.
When a delivery arrived damaged last winter he telephoned the supplier himself and had it replaced before the manager knew about it.
I would employ him again without hesitating.
writing.criteria: At least two superlatives, each with the; at least one specific incident as evidence; one honest qualification that is fairly explained; a clear closing judgement
writing.support: Write the incident first. A reference is built around one thing the person actually did, and the adjectives are chosen afterwards to match it. Starting from adjectives produces Reference B.
writing.extension: Rewrite it as Reference B — remove every superlative, every incident and every judgement, and keep only what can be confirmed. Read both and notice how much damage the second one does without saying anything negative.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two references
writing.prompt:
Use the two references in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. Reference A says she is not as shy as she seems. What does that mean?
2. Reference B says her work was satisfactory. What is that telling you?
3. Which reference helps Sara more? Name two specific things that make the difference.
4. Reference A says she is quieter than most people here. Why is that not a criticism?
5. Reference B criticises nothing at all. Explain how it still damages her.
writing.model:
1. It means she is less shy than she appears. She seems shy, but the reason is that she waits to be asked rather than that she is uncomfortable.
2. Very little that is good. Satisfactory is the lowest acceptable word, and it is chosen when the writer does not want to praise but does not want to criticise either.
3. Reference A. It uses superlatives — the most reliable member of the team — and it gives evidence, such as reporting her own mistake before anybody noticed.
4. Because it is immediately explained and then corrected: she is sometimes shy with new staff but not as shy as she seems. A fair qualification makes the praise around it more believable.
5. By what it leaves out. It confirms dates, uses the weakest positive word available, says she did what she was told, and makes no judgement about employing her again. A reader notices every one of those absences.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 identifies satisfactory as faint praise; answer 3 names two specific features; answer 5 explains damage by omission rather than by criticism
writing.support: Read Reference B twice and underline everything that is a fact rather than a judgement. Almost all of it will be underlined, and that is the finding.
writing.extension: Rewrite Reference B so it says exactly the same facts but would genuinely help her. What did you have to add?

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. She is biggest person on the team.
2. He works very good.
3. She is a carefully driver.
4. This job is as harder as the last one.
5. It is the most biggest warehouse in the town.
6. She is tall with dark hair. (asked: what is she like?)
7. This job is similar as my last one.
8. He drives very careful.
writing.model:
1. She is the biggest person on the team. (Pattern 2 — the is not optional with a superlative)
2. He works very well. (Pattern 3 — the adverb of good is well, not good)
3. She is a careful driver. (Pattern 3 — driver is a thing, so it takes the adjective)
4. This job is as hard as the last one. (Pattern 4 — the adjective inside as … as never changes)
5. It is the biggest warehouse in the town. (Pattern 2 — use -est or the most, never both)
6. She is kind and very calm. (Pattern 1 — what is she like asks for character, not appearance)
7. This job is similar to my last one. (Pattern 4 — similar takes to)
8. He drives very carefully. (Pattern 3 — drives is an action, so it takes the adverb)
writing.criteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; number 6 replaces appearance with character rather than fixing grammar
writing.support: Numbers 3 and 8 are the same pattern in opposite directions — an adverb where an adjective belongs, and an adjective where an adverb belongs. Fix them as a pair and the rule becomes visible.
writing.extension: Number 6 was grammatically perfect and answered the wrong question. Write two more like it, one for each of the other two questions.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Character or appearance?
activities.instructions:
Write CHARACTER or APPEARANCE for each word.
1. kind
2. tall
3. honest
4. curly
5. lazy
6. thin
7. confident
8. smart
9. generous
10. with glasses
11. shy
12. with a beard
activities.answers:
CHARACTER: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
APPEARANCE: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
Number 8 is the one that catches people. Smart here means well dressed, which is appearance. In some places smart means clever, which would be character — so if you wrote CHARACTER, you were not wrong about the word, only about which meaning this course teaches.
Character words answer what is she like. Appearance words answer what does she look like.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Superlatives
activities.instructions:
Write the superlative of the word in brackets.
1. It is ____ (big) warehouse in the town.
2. She is ____ (reliable) person on the team.
3. That was ____ (good) interview I have had.
4. This is ____ (easy) part of the job.
5. It was ____ (bad) day of the week.
6. That is ____ (expensive) one in the shop.
7. He is ____ (funny) person here.
8. This is ____ (busy) time of year.
9. She is ____ (kind) person I know.
10. It is ____ (difficult) thing about the job.
11. That is ____ (cheap) way to travel.
12. He is ____ (confident) speaker in the group.
activities.answers:
1. the biggest  2. the most reliable  3. the best  4. the easiest  5. the worst  6. the most expensive  7. the funniest  8. the busiest  9. the kindest  10. the most difficult  11. the cheapest  12. the most confident
Every answer begins with the. Count yours — if any is missing, that is the error to drill.
Spelling to check: biggest doubles the g; easiest, funniest and busiest all change y to i.
Short words took -est in 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 11. Long words took the most in 2, 6, 10 and 12.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Adjective or adverb?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form.
1. She is a (careful / carefully) driver.
2. She drives (careful / carefully).
3. He works (quick / quickly).
4. He is a (quick / quickly) worker.
5. He is a (good / well) worker.
6. He works (good / well).
7. She spoke (polite / politely).
8. She is a (polite / politely) person.
9. The first day went (bad / badly).
10. It was a (bad / badly) day.
11. He speaks very (quiet / quietly).
12. He has a (quiet / quietly) voice.
activities.answers:
1. careful  2. carefully  3. quickly  4. quick  5. good  6. well  7. politely  8. polite  9. badly  10. bad  11. quietly  12. quiet
The twelve are six pairs. In each pair, one describes a thing — driver, worker, person, day, voice — and takes the adjective. The other describes an action — drives, works, spoke, went, speaks — and takes the adverb.
If you got any wrong, find the word being described before choosing. That single step decides every one of them.
Numbers 5 and 6 are the irregular: good describes the worker, well describes the working.

activities.title: Practice 4 — As … as
activities.instructions:
Write each sentence.
1. Two jobs, equally hard.
2. This job, less hard than the last one.
3. She and her brother, equally tall.
4. Two prices, exactly equal. Use the same.
5. Two jobs, nearly but not quite equally difficult.
6. Two jobs that resemble each other. Use similar.
7. Two jobs that do not resemble each other. Use different.
8. This week, less busy than last week.
activities.answers:
1. This job is as hard as the last one.
2. This job is not as hard as the last one.
3. She is as tall as her brother.
4. It costs exactly the same as the other one.
5. It is almost as difficult as the last one.
6. This job is similar to the one I did before.
7. This job is different from the one I did before.
8. This week is not as busy as last week.
In 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 the adjective is plain — hard, tall, difficult, busy. No -er and no more, ever, inside as … as.
Numbers 4, 6 and 7 are the three prepositions: the same as, similar to, different from. Say those three together until the pairing is automatic.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Describe somebody so they can be found
activities.instructions:
Think of a public place you know — a station, a market, a waiting room.
Write a description of somebody so that a stranger could find them there. Four sentences.
Use only appearance words, and use has, is and with at least once each.
Then write one sentence saying why appearance words are the right choice here, using the test from Reading 2.
Do not use a real person's name.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your description.
What most people find: three or four features are enough, and the useful ones are the ones visible from a distance. Height, hair, and one item of clothing will find almost anybody. Eye colour, which people often include, is useless at ten metres.
The second finding is about the test in Reading 2. This description has a job to do, which is why appearance words are appropriate here and would not be if you were telling somebody what a new colleague is like.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Listen for a superlative
activities.instructions:
This week, listen for three superlatives in real speech — in a conversation, on the radio, in an advertisement.
Write each one down exactly as you heard it.
Then note whether it used -est or the most, and whether the was there.
Advertisements are the easiest place to find them, and the most exaggerated.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: the is always there in real speech, even when speakers drop other small words. That is worth seeing with your own examples, because it is the error this unit most wants to prevent.
The second finding is that superlatives in advertisements are usually unprovable — the best, the freshest, the most popular — and no evidence follows. Compare that with Reference A in Reading 3, where every superlative is followed by an incident. That difference is what makes one persuasive and the other noise.

quizzes.q: Somebody asks: what is she like? What are they asking about?
quizzes.why: The verb is is, so this asks what kind of person she is. What does she look like asks about appearance, and what does she like asks about preferences.

options: She is biggest person on the team.
She is more biggest person on the team.
She is the biggest person on the team.
She is most biggest person on the team.
quizzes.a: She is the biggest person on the team.
quizzes.why: The is required with every superlative, and you use either -est or the most but never both.
Drives is an action, and actions take the adverb. The adverb is formed by adding -ly to the adjective.

quizzes.q: What is the adverb of good?
quizzes.why: This is the one irregular adverb you will use constantly. He is a good worker, but he works well.

options: This job is as harder as the last one.
This job is as more hard as the last one.
This job is as hard as the last one.
This job is as hardest as the last one.
quizzes.a: This job is as hard as the last one.
quizzes.why: The adjective inside as … as never changes. No -er, no -est, no more — the structure itself does the comparing.

quizzes.q: This job is not as hard as the last one. What does it mean?
quizzes.why: Not as … as means less than. It says exactly what easier says, and English uses it because it lands more gently.

quizzes.q: Which word takes the most rather than -est?
quizzes.why: Long words take the most. One-syllable words and two-syllable words ending in -y take -est — so biggest, easiest and cheapest.

options: This job is similar to my last one.
This job is similar as my last one.
This job is similar from my last one.
This job is similar than my last one.
quizzes.a: This job is similar to my last one.
quizzes.why: The three related words each take a different preposition: the same as, similar to, different from.
Driver is a thing, and things take the adjective. Only actions take the -ly form.

quizzes.q: Reference B says her work was satisfactory. What does that communicate?
options: Faint praise — it is the lowest acceptable word
That there was a complaint about her
quizzes.a: Faint praise — it is the lowest acceptable word
quizzes.why: Nothing in Reference B is a criticism, and that is the point. It is chosen when the writer will not praise but will not criticise either, and readers notice.

quizzes.q: What is the adverb of easy?
quizzes.why: Adjectives ending in y change to -ily. The same change happens in the superlative: the easiest.

quizzes.q: Which sentence correctly answers what does she look like?
options: She is kind and quite shy.
She has short dark hair and wears glasses.
She is the most reliable person here.
quizzes.a: She has short dark hair and wears glasses.
quizzes.why: Look like asks for appearance, which uses has, is and with. The other three answer the character question, the preferences question, and the character question again.

teacherNotes.note: Four pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key. Practice 3 is the diagnostic and it is built as six pairs so a learner can see the rule emerge from their own answers rather than being told it again. Practices 5 and 6 are field tasks with no key, and both carry a what-most-people-find note so a solo learner still gets feedback.

teacherNotes.type: Three questions taught as a set
teacherNotes.note: What is she like, what does she look like and what does she like are five words each and one word apart. Taught separately they are permanently confusing; taught together in one card they are usually fixed in a single session. Reading 1 exists for this and Speaking 1 drills all three in one recording.

teacherNotes.type: Appearance vocabulary is handled carefully on purpose
teacherNotes.note: Reading 2 gives a test of purpose — is this description doing a job? — rather than a list of forbidden words. Every appearance task in the unit has an identifying purpose built in, including Practice 5, which asks the learner to describe somebody so a stranger could find them. The word thin appears with identifying examples only, and its opposite is not taught at all. That is a deliberate choice and the reasoning is stated in the reading rather than hidden.

teacherNotes.type: Superlatives are a Unit 4 extension, not new material
teacherNotes.note: The short-and-long rule, the three spelling changes and the irregulars are all identical to the comparatives in Unit 4. If a learner struggles here, check Unit 4 first — the problem is almost always the underlying short-or-long judgement rather than the superlative itself. The genuinely new thing is the, which is the error Speaking 3 and Practice 2 are built to catch.

teacherNotes.type: Why two references rather than one
teacherNotes.note: Reference B contains no criticism whatsoever and is still damaging, which is a harder reading skill than spotting a negative statement. Four of the ten comprehension questions turn on what is absent — no superlative, no incident, no closing judgement. Writing 2's extension asks the learner to convert A into B themselves, which is the fastest way to see how the damage is done.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Writing 1 and Speaking 2 ask learners to describe real colleagues, and Practice 5 asks for a description of a person in a public place: no real names, workplaces or identifying details should be collected, shared or entered into the app. Practice 5 says explicitly not to use a real person's name, and that wording should stay.

selfAssessment.statement: I can describe what a person is like and what they look like, and tell the two questions apart.
I can say the biggest, the most expensive and the best without hesitating.
I can say she is a careful driver and she drives carefully, and know which one a sentence needs.
I can say as tall as and not as hard as, and read what a reference implies.

assignment.title: A person described, and two references judged
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record a description of somebody you know in two halves — six sentences of character only including at least one superlative, then three sentences of appearance only using has, is and with — and finish by recording one sentence saying which half was harder to keep separate and why. Second, write full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3 about the two references in Reading 3, and add a rewritten version of Reference B that states the same facts but would genuinely help her, with one line saying what you had to add. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written answers
